exhibits.source: Taittirīya Upaniṣad & Īśā Upaniṣad Śānti Pāṭha
exhibits.curatorialNote: The invocation establishes an ontological safety container. Unlike competitive scholastic debate, the Vedic dialogue begins with reciprocal protection (saha nāvavatu) and mathematical completeness (pūrṇam adaḥ).
exhibits.audioGuideText: Welcome to the Prologue. In the Upanishadic tradition, every inquiry begins with peace invocations. Before addressing suffering or resilience, teacher and student synchronize their attention in shared ontological safety.

exhibits.source: Comparative Epistemology: Vedic & Modern Cognitive Science
exhibits.curatorialNote: Modern resilience often measures systemic rebound after acute stress. The Upanishadic paradigm proposes that the underlying observing ground never fractured in the first place.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room One contrasts two paradigms of the human mind: modern resilience as bouncing back, versus the Upanishadic discovery of an unshakeable ground that never fell.

exhibits.curatorialNote: The word Upaniṣad derives from upa (near), ni (down), and ṣad (to sit). It marks a revolutionary pedagogical shift from external fire rituals to interior self-investigation.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Two documents the corpus of the ten principal Upanishads, marking the historical transition from sacrificial altars to the quiet fire of inner awareness.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.2 offers one of antiquity's most rigorous formulations of existential dread: 'Dvitīyād vai bhayaṃ bhavati'—fear arises exclusively from the perception of a second.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Three examines fearlessness, or abhaya. The sage declares that fear can only exist when reality is bifurcated into subject and threat. Dissolve the imagined boundary, and fear has nowhere to land.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Nachiketa sits for three days and nights without food at the portal of Death (Yama). When offered empires and immortal pleasures, the youth demands only the secret of the Self.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Four enters the realm of Yama. A young boy faces death itself, rejecting every temporal bribe to uncover that which survives the dissolution of the body.

exhibits.curatorialNote: The chariot allegorizes human executive architecture: the Self is the passenger, the body the carriage, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, the mind the reins, and the senses the horses.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Five unpacks the famous chariot metaphor of self-regulation. Mastery is not the suppression of the senses, but their intelligent guidance by a clear and steady intellect.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Nārada has mastered all four Vedas, astronomy, politics, and the fine arts, yet confesses to Sanatkumāra: 'I am full of grief; guide me across sorrow.' Information alone cannot liberate.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Six presents the encounter between Nārada and Sanatkumāra. Despite encyclopedic knowledge, sorrow persists until the infinite, Bhūmā, is directly realized.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Through nine pedagogical metaphors—dissolved salt, the banyan seed, rivers merging into the ocean—Uddālaka demonstrates to Śvetaketu that identity is continuous with the cosmos.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Seven demonstrates Tat Tvam Asi: That Thou Art. When transient social roles collapse, the subtle ground remains undestroyed, like salt invisibly pervading water.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Titikṣā is deliberate, patient endurance without retaliatory resentment or depressive collapse. Complemented by the thunder-syllable DA: self-control, generosity, and compassion.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Eight explores titikṣā, or noble endurance. Here resilience is not numb stoicism, but radiant patience anchored in an inner sanctuary.

exhibits.curatorialNote: The human organism consists of five concentric sheaths: physical nourishment, vital energy, mental emotions, discerning wisdom, and bliss. Suffering arises when identity is glued to an outer sheath.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Nine diagrams the Panchakosha: the five sheaths of human experience, showing how distress at the physical or emotional layer does not contaminate the witness.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Two birds sit in the selfsame tree: one pecks the sweet and bitter berries of experience; the other looks on in silence without tasting. Māṇḍūkya unveils Turīya: the fourth beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Ten introduces the silent witness. One bird grieves over transient fruits; the higher bird watches serenely, untouched by the tempest of circumstantial fortune.

exhibits.curatorialNote: 'Nāyam ātmā balahīnena labhyaḥ'—this Self cannot be attained by the weak. Spiritual awakening demands robust cognitive courage, laser-like focus, and unyielding truth.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Eleven celebrates existential strength. The Upanishads repudiate spiritual escapism; realization is an arrow drawn on the bow of meditation and shot directly into reality.

exhibits.curatorialNote: 'Mana eva manuṣyāṇāṃ kāraṇaṃ bandha-mokṣayoḥ'—the mind alone is the cause of bondage and freedom. Attached to sensory objects it binds; freed from grasping it liberates.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Twelve probes the mechanics of mental sovereignty. The mind is an instrument, not a master; when calibrated with discernment, it becomes the gateway to peace.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Envelop all this changing world with the sacred; enjoy through renunciation; covet not anyone's wealth. Perform work for a hundred years without collapsing under existential fatigue.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Thirteen solves the paradox of action. How to live vigorously in the world for a full lifespan without despair: engage wholeheartedly while relinquishing possessive clinging.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Maitreyī asks: 'What will not make me immortal, what should I do with that?' Gārgī Vācaknavī challenges the greatest philosopher of the court with relentless cosmic cross-examination.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Fourteen honors the women philosophers of the Upanishads. Maitreyī rejects material wealth for existential truth, and Gārgī fearlessly interrogates the boundaries of the cosmos.

exhibits.curatorialNote: A practical synthesis of contemplative technology: Śravaṇa (listening), Manana (reflection), and Nididhyāsana (deep meditative assimilation). Note: educational, not clinical psychotherapy.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Fifteen provides a contemplative toolkit for modern daily life: sound meditation, witness reflection, and cognitive reframing drawn from ancient inquiries.

exhibits.curatorialNote: Honest scholarship demands recognizing historical context, theological diversity between Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita, and the clinical hazard of spiritual bypassing.
exhibits.audioGuideText: Room Sixteen provides critical perspective, warning against spiritual bypassing and acknowledging historical boundaries to preserve academic integrity.

exhibits.curatorialNote: 'Asato mā sad gamaya; tamaso mā jyotir gamaya; mṛtyor mā amṛtaṃ gamaya.' The timeless ascent from illusion to truth, darkness to light, and death to the immortal Self.
exhibits.audioGuideText: The final chamber culminates in the grand prayer: Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality. The journey resolves in golden sunrise.
